**Short answer:** Nvidia closed at $117.59, down 6.38% on the day [E1]. The company reported record quarterly revenue of $30,040 million, up 15% from the prior quarter and up 122% from a year earlier [E9]. The filings show no collapse in demand. The drop reflects a narrow beat against high expectations, a lower gross margin, and a next-quarter outlook that investors did not read as a step up. Reuters said the forecast was largely in line and that the stock fell over 6% [E6]. Nothing retrieved shows the AI trade breaking down, but one session and one company's report cannot establish a sector trend.

**Reported results**

- Revenue: $30,040 million, up 15% from the prior quarter and up 122% from a year earlier [E9]
- Data Center revenue: $26.3 billion, a record, up 16% from the prior quarter and up 154% from a year earlier [E5]
- Non-GAAP diluted EPS: $0.68, up 11% from the prior quarter and up 152% from a year earlier [E5]
- Non-GAAP gross margin: 75.7%, down 3.2 points from 78.9% in the prior quarter [E9]

The sequential gross margin decline was attributed to inventory provisions for low-yielding Blackwell material and a higher mix of new products in Data Center [E9]. Next-quarter non-GAAP gross margin is guided to 75.0%, plus or minus 50 basis points [E9]. Blackwell production is scheduled to ramp in the fourth quarter, with several billion dollars of Blackwell revenue expected that quarter [E9].

**Why the stock fell**

Reuters described the forecast as largely in line and said it disappointed investors used to beats by wide margins [E6]. Markets Insider, a tier 4 source, called the beat the narrowest in six quarters and cited more complex products as a concern [E7]. I could not retrieve consensus revenue and EPS estimates, so the size of the beat against expectations is unverified.

The evidence points to a sentiment reset around one company, not a broken demand story. Sequential revenue still grew 15% and Data Center revenue hit a record [E9][E5]. The broader market was not in distress: the S&P 500 ended roughly flat and the Dow closed at a record [E6].

**Limits**

The 8-K index and body text were not captured, so the press release and CFO commentary were read through their exhibit URLs [E8][E9]. Consensus estimates and a numeric revenue outlook were not retrieved. Alpha Vantage earnings data failed validation, so no independent estimate data is used. results.finalAssistantText:
**Short answer:** On and Hoka are taking real share, but the filings suggest they explain only part of Nike's stall. The stock looks expensive on trailing earnings for a business with flat revenue, so "bargain" isn't supported yet.

**Did On and Hoka steal Nike's lunch?**

- Hoka's wholesale sales rose to $1,126.1m in the year to March 2024 [E14], up 21.63% from $925.9m [E14, C2]. Its direct-to-consumer sales aren't broken out in the retrieved data, so the total is understated.
- Nike's FY24 revenue was $51.4bn [E12] against $51.2bn [E3], up 0.36% [C1]. Hoka's wholesale gain of about $200m [C6] was larger than Nike's entire $183m revenue increase [C5].
- Hoka's wholesale sales were about 2.19% of Nike's FY24 revenue [C4], so it can't account for the whole problem.
- Nike's Q4 NIKE Direct revenue fell 8% on a reported basis [E12]. That points to Nike's own channels and execution as a major driver, not only lost wholesale accounts. The filings don't isolate how much share On and Hoka took.
- On's 2023 revenue rose 46.64% to CHF 1,792.1m [E16, C7]. That is much smaller than Nike's $49.3bn NIKE Brand revenue [E12].

**Bargain or trap?**

- At $75.43 [E2], Nike trades at 20.22x trailing EPS [C8]. That EPS figure, $3.73 [A1], is my sum of reported quarters, not a reported annual number.
- FY24 EPS rose 15.48% [C9] on flat revenue. Q4 gross margin rose 110 basis points to 44.7% [E12] on pricing and lower freight and warehousing costs [E12]. The earnings gain came from margins and costs, not growth.
- Morningstar cut its fair value to $124 [E7] from $129 after Q4, citing a projected mid-single-digit sales decline in FY25 [E7]. That is a third-party view.

**What I could not verify**

- The "5-year low" claim. The price-history request failed, so no price series is in evidence.
- Nike's FY25 outlook text. The 8-K exhibit's guidance section didn't come back, so the decline rests on the Morningstar summary alone.
- The "nobody wears them" impression from the mall. That is an anecdote, not evidence on share.

**What would change the view:** If Nike's Direct sales and North American revenue stabilise and revenue turns positive while margins hold, the bargain case gains weight. If Direct and North America keep falling and the guided FY25 decline arrives, the trap case gains weight. If Hoka and On keep growing wholesale near Hoka's FY24 pace of 21.63% [C2] while Nike's wholesale stays flat, the competitive explanation strengthens. The next filings to check are Nike's FY25 Q1 10-Q and its guidance text.

This is research, not investment advice.

- Nike's Q4 FY24 revenue fell 2% reported and was flat currency-neutral [E9]. Full-year revenue was $51.4 billion, up 1% currency-neutral [E9].
- NIKE Direct fell 8% to $5.1 billion, while wholesale rose 5% to $7.1 billion [E9]. That's the pattern you'd expect if Nike is losing full-price, own-channel demand, but it doesn't prove competitors caused it.

- Fiscal 2025 guidance and Q1 FY25 results, to see whether the revenue decline is mid-single-digit and gross margin holds above 44%. I couldn't confirm guidance from the release body.

- Strategy held about 386,700 bitcoin as of 2024-11-24, bought at an aggregate $21.9 billion, or about $56,761 per coin [E8].

- Debt maturities, put dates, conversion terms, covenants and preferred dividend obligations. These decide whether a drawdown forces a sale or a default.

- The bitcoin spot quote is from the market data feed [E2], but its link to the report's coverage figures is flagged as unverified in the report.
